Stalin. Born in Georgia as Iosif Dzhugashvili, Stalin adopted the pseudonym meaning "man of steel" as a revolutionary. From 1878 to 1953, he was the totalitarian dictator of the Soviet Union who transformed it into an industrial superpower while perpetrating some of history's most systematic atrocities. After Lenin's death in 1924, Stalin outmaneuvered rival Leon Trotsky for control of the Bolshevik Party through cunning political maneuvering and alliance-building. Stalin's policy of collectivization forced peasants into collective farms. Agricultural chaos and deliberate requisitions triggered the Holodomor, a man-made famine killing millions in Ukraine. The Great Purge from 1936 to 1938 saw Stalin eliminate suspected enemies within the Communist Party, military, and intelligentsia. Hundreds of thousands were executed or sent to gulags. Stalin rebuilt the Soviet military and industrialized the economy through brutal Five-Year Plans, prioritizing heavy industry and military capacity over consumer goods. During World War II, Stalin mobilized the Soviet Union against Nazi Germany. Soviet sacrifice proved decisive in defeating fascism, though the war cost over twenty-seven million Soviet lives. After 1945, Stalin imposed communist regimes throughout Eastern Europe and confronted the Western Allies in the nascent Cold War. He ruled the Soviet state through totalitarian control for a quarter-century, rising to power through ruthless consolidation of authority. Stalin perfected the system of absolute state control through propaganda, terror, and ideology, ultimately becoming a paramount figure in the Cold War that followed his death.
